sections.h1: Dashboards that actually get used. Insights, explained. Data your whole team can act on.
sections.standfirst: Whether you are tracking core SaaS metrics or sending the monthly update that explains why a number moved, Metabase gives your team somewhere to build reporting and somewhere to read it.
sections.h2: Interactive, collaborative, and built for data pros and non-technical people
sections.sub: Straightforward tools for everyone to create, structure, and use dashboards and reports on their own.

cards.title: Interactive dashboards
cards.body: Assemble a dashboard out of saved questions and filters to follow the numbers that move fastest, then let people change the date range or the segment themselves rather than queueing for someone to rebuild it. Charts respond to clicks, so the follow-up question is usually one menu away, and you can hand the whole thing to a team without handing over your afternoon.
cards.trailingLabel: Learn more about dashboards in Metabase.

cards.title: Documents
cards.body: Put the visualizations next to the writing that explains them, so a chart turns up with the reason it matters attached instead of on its own. Documents are the difference between sending a number and sending an argument, which is what most monthly updates are really trying to be. Write once, embed the live charts, and let the text update around them.
cards.trailingLabel: Learn more about Documents in Metabase.

cards.title: Sharing data with your team and customers
cards.body: Send dashboards to where people already are rather than asking them to come and find one. A direct link, a scheduled email, a Slack message on a Monday morning, or an embed inside your own product for the customers who should only see their own rows. Each route carries the same permissions, so sharing never quietly widens access.
cards.trailingLabel: Learn more about sharing in Metabase.

sections.h2b: Get better at building analytics dashboards

linkCards.title: Building Metabase dashboards like a pro
From zero to dashboard in 6 mins

faqs.question: How do dashboards help teams make data-driven decisions?
faqs.answer: A dashboard puts the handful of numbers a team actually steers by in one place, refreshed from the database rather than pasted in. That turns the weekly argument about whose figures are right into a conversation about what to do next.

faqs.question: What's the best way to share a dashboard with non-technical teammates?
faqs.answer: Send a link or set up a subscription that emails or Slacks it on a schedule. Neither asks the recipient to learn the tool, and both keep the permissions you already set, so nobody sees more than they should.

faqs.question: Can I create data reports that tell a story, not just show charts?
faqs.answer: That is what Documents are for. You write the explanation and embed the live visualizations inside it, so the narrative and the numbers stay together and the numbers stay current.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a dashboard and a data report?
faqs.answer: A dashboard is for monitoring: the same questions, answered again whenever you open it. A report is for explaining a particular thing once, with the writing that makes sense of it.

faqs.question: How do I set up self-service analytics for my team?
faqs.answer: Curate the tables people see, add the metadata that makes the column names mean something, and give them the query builder. Most questions then get answered without reaching you at all.

faqs.question: How can I automate sharing dashboards and reports in Metabase?
faqs.answer: Dashboard subscriptions send a dashboard by email or Slack on a schedule, and alerts fire when a result crosses a threshold, so people hear about a change without watching for it.

sections.ctaBody: Give your team the open source reporting tool they will actually enjoy using.

seo.metaDescription: Organize models, questions and dashboards into collections, set permissions per group, and mark the reviewed ones official.

sections.standfirst: Bring some structure to your Metabase by tucking related models, questions and dashboards together into collections, and make the good ones easy to find.
sections.sub: As everyone explores and adds more to your Metabase, things get noisy. These are the tools that keep it in check.

cards.title: Collections
cards.body: Give each team its own corner of Metabase and bundle everything they need into it, with sub-collections when one corner is not enough.

cards.title: Collection permissions
cards.body: Grant view access, curate access, or none at all, and set it separately on a sub-collection when the parent is too broad.

cards.title: Official collections
cards.body: Admins can mark a collection official, so people can tell at a glance which numbers have been through review and which are someone’s working draft.

cards.title: Verified questions
cards.body: Put a blue check on the questions and models that have been looked over, so people can tell what has been reviewed, and let search rank the verified ones above everything else when someone goes hunting.

cards.title: Pin important items
cards.body: Keep the dashboards people actually open at the top of the collection, instead of three screens down an alphabetical list.

cards.title: Personal collection
cards.body: Somewhere to think out loud. Your personal collection is yours alone until you decide to move something out of it.

sections.h2b: More about collections and verified items
sections.howtoTitle: How to create a collection, set permissions, and mark it as official

howtoSteps.text: Create one with New > Collection, then move in the questions and dashboards that belong together.
Or start from a question: save it, and either pick a collection or create one from the bottom of the same menu.
If you are an admin, set and adjust permissions per group from the … menu at the top right.
Admins on a Pro or Enterprise plan can mark the collection Official from that same menu.

sections.ctaBody: Collections come with every plan. Marking them official needs Pro or Enterprise.

cards.title: Zoom in
cards.body: Find out why a number moved around a particular date by clicking and dragging across the part of the chart that looks interesting, and Metabase re-runs the question zoomed in on it.

cards.title: View these records
cards.body: Get to the specifics: click through to a table of the individual rows that make up the point you were looking at.

cards.title: Breakout
cards.body: Split the same measure by another dimension — time, location, category — without going back to the query builder.

cards.title: Filters
cards.body: Slice it a different way by clicking to apply a filter, and see what is actually high or low once the rows nobody asked about are out of the way.

cards.title: Custom click behavior
cards.body: Decide where the next click goes: a related dashboard, a saved question, or a URL in another system entirely.

cards.title: Cross-filter
cards.body: Wire a card to the dashboard’s filter widgets, so clicking a state on a map narrows every other card to it.

cards.title: X-ray
cards.body: Generate a whole dashboard of questions about a table or a single record automatically, then throw away the cards that were not interesting and keep the handful that turned out to be worth watching.

sections.h2b: More info on drill-throughs and interactivity
sections.howtoTitle: How to use drill-throughs on dashboards and charts

howtoSteps.text: Find a dashboard, chart or model you want to know more about.
Click anywhere on a chart built with the query builder — a state on a map, a bar in a bar chart, a slice of a pie — and pick whichever option from the drill-through menu looks like the next question.
That is more or less it. Go wild.

seo.metaDescription: Granular permissions by group, down to the row and column, with data sandboxing, collection permissions and download controls.

sections.h1: Fine-grained control over what people can see and do with data
sections.standfirst: Granular governance over what each group can reach, across your internal and your embedded analytics, right down to the row and the column.
sections.h2: From top secret to unrestricted access
sections.sub: With several layers in between. Decide what people see per database, schema, table, row or column.

cards.title: Manage permissions by group
cards.body: People can belong to more than one group. Where groups overlap, the most permissive setting is the one that applies, which keeps the rules predictable.

cards.title: Row and column level permissions
cards.body: Use data segregation to scope a table to one tenant, so the same saved question returns only the rows that belong to whoever ran it.

cards.title: Database-managed row-level permissions
cards.body: Map user attributes onto roles your database already defines, and let the privileges you maintain there carry straight through.

cards.title: Collection permissions
cards.body: Decide which groups can view or edit the questions, dashboards and models inside a collection.

cards.title: Application permissions
cards.body: Grant a group some administrative powers without making everyone an admin.

cards.title: Download results
cards.body: Control whether a group can export results from a given data source at all, and in what form.

sections.ctaBody: Get full control over how your data is reached and used, on every plan.

seo.metaDescription: Build questions from clicks and menus: filters, summaries, joins, custom expressions and multi-level aggregation, with no SQL required.

sections.h1: Get answers in a few clicks with the query builder
sections.standfirst: The query builder lets anyone — including your less data-savvy teammates — put a question together from clicks and menu choices, with no SQL anywhere in sight.
sections.sub: A point-and-click tool for people who do not write SQL, and a shortcut for the people who do.

cards.title: Filters and summarizations
cards.body: Narrow the data and group it from a dropdown, without having to remember what the column was called.

cards.title: Joins
cards.body: Ask questions about data that lives across more than one table or model, and let Metabase work out the keys where it can.

cards.title: Custom expressions
cards.body: Go past the basics with expressions that work the way spreadsheet formulas do, so the syntax is already familiar.

cards.title: Multi-level aggregation
cards.body: Summarize a summary. Stack another filter or grouping on top of a result you have already aggregated.

cards.title: Preview results
cards.body: Check what a filter is doing as you add it, without running the whole query against the whole table.

cards.title: Question history
cards.body: Let anyone edit a question while Metabase keeps the versions, so a change that turns out wrong is one click from being undone.

sections.h2b: More about asking questions in Metabase
sections.howtoTitle: How to ask a question with the query builder

howtoSteps.text: Click New > Question at the top right of your Metabase to open the query builder. You can also get to it from a saved question by clicking the editor icon, which is quicker than starting again when all you want is a small change to something that already exists.
Pick the table or model you want to ask about — say the Orders table from the sample data that ships with Metabase.
Click into Filters, choose Created at, and select Last 12 months.
Click + to add another filter. This time choose Total, then pick Greater than from the dropdown, and enter a number to cut off the small orders.
Click into Summarize, choose Sum of…, and pick Taxes as the column to add up.
Use the by box beside it to group the results. Start with Product > Category.
Click + to group by Created at as well, and choose month.
Hit Visualize. You get a chart showing how tax splits across product categories on orders, month by month, which is the question you just described.

sections.ctaBody: The query builder is on every plan, and you can embed it for customer-facing analytics on Pro or Enterprise.

sections.h2b: More about asking questions in Metabase
sections.howtoTitle: How to ask a question with SQL

howtoSteps.text: Click New > SQL Query at the top of Metabase. You will not see this option at all if your group has not been given native query access, which is deliberate — it is the setting that decides who gets to write raw SQL.
Write your query. If you are here, you know what to do — we will stay out of the way.
Click the run button to see the results below.
To turn them into a chart, click Visualization and pick whatever fits the shape of the data, clicking through the options to see each one applied.
Save it, put it in a collection or on a dashboard, share it, and carry on.

sections.ctaBody: Get more granular access to your data with the SQL editor.

cards.title: Usage reports, configuration changes and audit logs
cards.body: Comprehensive records of how your Metabase is being used, by whom and when, which is usually what compliance is asking for.

cards.title: Interactive pre-defined dashboards
cards.body: Overall trends without building anything yourself: which dashboards get viewed most, which questions run slowest, who is active this month and who has quietly stopped logging in at all.

cards.title: Models to create custom reports
cards.body: Your usage and audit data arrives already modelled, so asking a new question of it does not mean learning a new schema.

cards.title: Set up subscriptions and alerts
cards.body: Get a regular digest, or an alarm when something changes unexpectedly and you would rather know now than at the end of the month.

cards.title: Customize prebuilt dashboards
cards.body: The audit logs are read-only by default so they stay trustworthy and nobody can quietly edit the record, but you can duplicate any dashboard into your own collection and reshape that copy freely.

cards.title: Manage access to usage analytics
cards.body: Give view or edit access where it is needed, without handing out admin to everyone who wants a number.

sections.h2b: Get the most out of usage analytics

linkCards.title: Learn what's happening in your Metabase…using Metabase

howtoSteps.text: Open the Metabase analytics collection in the left sidebar. Admins see it by default; others need to be given access.

Open Metabase metrics, pick a date range, and filter by the user groups you have. You could narrow it to one team to see which dashboards they actually open, and which ones nobody has touched since they were built.
Set up a dashboard subscription so the answer arrives every week without anyone going to look for it.

sections.h2: Key features of our white-labeled embedded analytics
sections.sub: Customization that covers what you need now, with developer tooling for when that changes.

cards.title: Branded in-app reporting
cards.body: Set the name, the logo, the fonts, and the UI and chart colours, so the reporting area reads as a part of your product rather than a window into someone else’s.

cards.title: Hide all traces of Metabase
cards.body: Point help links at your own documentation, swap the illustrations, and leave nothing that says this came from somewhere else.

cards.title: No-code customization
cards.body: Restyle the embedded views through configuration alone, without putting a front-end engineer on it.

cards.title: Go beyond white-labeling
cards.body: Use Modular Embedding or the SDK to place individual React components exactly where your own layout wants them, rather than fitting your page around one big embedded frame.

cards.title: Dynamic theming
cards.body: Style each component with CSS variables, so switching theme at runtime is a variable change rather than a rebuild.

cards.title: Customized UX
cards.body: Override menu names, button labels and placement to build click-paths that match how your customers already work.

sections.howtoTitle: How to set up white-label analytics in your app

howtoSteps.text: Choose your white-labeling method. Use Modular Embedding for a quick implementation, or the Modular Embedding SDK when you want control over how the components are composed inside your own layout.
Add your branding — logo, colours, fonts, and whatever custom UI elements you need.
Define permissions, and set up authentication so each customer only ever sees their own data.
Refine the user experience. With the SDK you can override menu names, button placement and tooltips, so the analytics feel native to your app.
Deploy, test with internal users, and iterate on the styling from there.

seo.metaDescription: Set strong boundaries around your multi-tenant data: row and column-level security, connection impersonation, database routing and locked parameters, compared.

sections.heading: Set strong boundaries around your multi-tenant data
sections.standfirst: Methods to fit your configuration preferences and your security requirements.

tabs.label: Row and column-level security
tabs.lede: Define rules in Metabase that limit which rows and columns each group can see, based on attributes you set.

tabs.label: Connection impersonation
tabs.lede: Database-managed row-level permissions: Metabase impersonates database roles to enforce what is visible, and still allows SQL editor access.

tabs.label: Database routing
tabs.lede: In one-database-per-tenant setups, Metabase routes each customer’s queries to their own database while shared content stays in a primary one.

tabs.label: Locked parameters
tabs.lede: Lightweight restriction for basic embedding, with locked parameters passed from your own app that the viewer cannot change.

columns.text: Tradeoffs / when it's not a fit

rows.name: Row-level security
rows.mean: Define rules inside Metabase that restrict which rows and columns people can see, based on attributes like user ID, group or region. They apply to questions and dashboards, not to native SQL.

when.text: You need granular control over what each person can see and use
You want control over access driven from the UI
You need flexible control per group or organisation

rows.example: For internal BI: west coast fleet managers at a nationwide logistics firm see only the fleet and delivery data for their own region.

tradeoffs.text: Does not apply to native or SQL queries
You are on a non-SQL database like Druid, though basic row-level security does work with MongoDB

rows.name: Connection impersonation
rows.mean: Metabase connects as the actual user or role in the database. You define the policies, roles and access controls there, and Metabase passes the identity through with SET ROLE.

when.text: You want the access logic centralised in the database
Native queries have to respect access control too
You are more worried about user attributes being misconfigured

rows.example: Set role-based permissions for users of your HR SaaS app, so a manager only ever sees data for their own direct reports.

tradeoffs.text: Adds complexity in user management and setup
Does not cache well in Metabase
Less friendly for smaller teams, or anyone who is not a DBA

rows.name: Database routing
rows.mean: When tenant data lives in separate databases, routing makes sure each tenant only ever sees results from theirs. Admins build the questions and dashboards once against a primary database.

when.text: You want the strongest isolation there is, which suits compliance and noisy-neighbour problems in multi-tenant embedding
You are more worried about user attributes being misconfigured
You want to avoid one tenant’s queries slowing another’s

rows.example: Acme's queries go to Acme's database when they open an embedded dashboard in your SaaS app, because the data is separated at the database level.

tradeoffs.text: Unnecessary if you do not need separation at the database level
Higher operational complexity, if you would rather manage permissions in the Metabase UI

rows.name: Locked parameters
rows.mean: Embed dashboards whose results are already filtered before they are shown, say to org_id = 123. The filter is invisible and cannot be tampered with, and is controlled by attributes from your host app.

when.text: Lightweight tenant isolation for embedded analytics
Simple access control that is still safe
Keeping a sensitive filter away from the people reading the dashboard

rows.example: On an embedded dashboard in your ecommerce app, show each seller their own sales using a hidden seller ID passed in by the host app.

tradeoffs.text: No user login, SSO or awareness of roles
Not something to rely on for high-risk data

sections.ctaBody: Keep sensitive, or simply irrelevant, data under wraps. Sandboxing and the rest of these methods are available on Pro and Enterprise plans, and you can try either without talking to anyone first.
